title: Extraordinary Lifetime Enhancement of Coherent Phonon-Amplitude Modes in the Excitonic Insulator Phase of Ta2Pd3Te5
authors: Anjan Kumar N M, Shuhan Wang, Snehashish Chatterjee, Yan Zhu, MinJae Kim, Tobias Ritschel, Elaheh Sadrollahi, Jochen Geck, Achim Rosch, Chandra Shekhar, Claudia Felser, Stefan Kaiser
abstract: The excitonic insulator (EI) is an electronic phase of condensed excitons. However, in many prototypical materials the presence of a concurrent structural transition complicates the identification of a purely electronic origin of the ordered state. Here, we investigate Ta2Pd3Te5, in which an EI phase develops below TC ~ 100 K in the absence of a detectable structural transition. We characterize the excitonic condensate via its coherent phonon-amplitude response. Most strikingly, an extraordinarily strong lifetime enhancement of these modes sets in below TC which we establish as a new and robust fingerprint linked to exciton condensation. We discuss possibilities to capture the enhancement when taking into account a coupling of excitonic and lattice effects in line with the coupled phonon-amplitude response. Within an order-parameter polaron picture coupling to the excitonic state may dress the phonon mode and thereby suppress its relaxation and a phenomenological model combines the anharmonic phonon response and a reduced electronic scattering due to the gap opening in the EI phase.
summary: This work investigates the excitonic insulator phase in $	ext{Ta}_2	ext{Pd}_3	ext{Te}_5$ by studying its coherent phonon modes. The key finding is an anomalous, strong lifetime enhancement of these phonons below the transition temperature, which is proposed to be a robust fingerprint of exciton condensation. The enhancement is quantitatively explained by modeling the phonon as an 'order-parameter polaron' coupled to the excitonic condensate fluctuations.
main_problem: To identify a robust, purely electronic fingerprint for the excitonic insulator (EI) phase in $	ext{Ta}_2	ext{Pd}_3	ext{Te}_5$, especially since the transition occurs without a detectable structural change.
main_result: The hallmark of exciton condensation is an extraordinarily strong, non-anharmonic lifetime enhancement observed in the coherent phonon-amplitude modes below the transition temperature ($T_C \approx 100 	ext{ K}$).
method: The study combines time-resolved pump-probe spectroscopy to measure phonon lifetimes and amplitudes with theoretical modeling using exciton-polaron and coupled phonon-exciton models.
model_or_system: The system is $	ext{Ta}_2	ext{Pd}_3	ext{Te}_5$, which enters an EI phase. The theoretical framework involves modeling the coherent phonon mode as coupling to the fluctuations of the excitonic order parameter, leading to an 'order-parameter polaron' description.
key_observables:
Coherent phonon lifetimes ($	au$), phonon frequencies ($
u$), and the temperature/fluence dependence of the lifetime enhancement factor ($\eta(T)$).
important_parameters: Transition temperature ($T_C \approx 100 	ext{ K}$), excitonic gap ($\Delta \approx 80 	ext{ meV}$), and the coupling strength ($\lambda$) derived from the polaron model.
main_assumptions: The enhancement is attributed to the coherent phonon being 'dressed' by the excitonic condensate fluctuations, and the analysis relies on fitting the data to specific polaron or coupled decay models.
figures_summary: Figures show the temperature dependence of phonon lifetimes, clearly illustrating a deviation from expected anharmonic decay below $T_C$. Theoretical fits using the exciton-polaron model successfully reproduce this anomalous lifetime enhancement.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the EI phase via transport/spectroscopy, then analyzes the temperature dependence of the phonon response, contrasting anharmonic predictions with the observed anomaly, and finally models this anomaly using the exciton-polaron framework.
why_interesting: The mechanism of lifetime enhancement due to coupling with a quantum condensate (exciton) provides a clean, measurable signature of an electronic phase transition, analogous to superconducting gap signatures in tunneling spectroscopy, making it relevant to open quantum systems dynamics.
